rv.q: Dirden's exquisite production, though, is both amusing and wise.

What's even more of a marvel than the arrival of this theatrical rara avis is the daffy splendidness of the Roundabout Theatre Company production, directed with an anything-for-a-guffaw spirit by Brandon J. Dirden, and featuring a scintillating cast preening and careening around the stage.
Even the most clown-phobic among us – and, yes, a little panto can indeed go a long way – might be won over anytime this rubber-limbed, clay-faced sui generis performer enters a room.
The production as a whole isn't always as crisp as Irwin himself.

Still, they just don't make 'em like Irwin anymore when it comes to outré farce and satire and 90 minutes watching this renowned thespian essay an old coot kicking and screaming as young people all around him point out his vulnerability and mortality was weirdly invigorating for me.

If this production fails to amuse, except in spurts, it isn’t the fault of Molière in general or even this play in particular: Off Broadway’s Red Bull Theater mounted an excellent account of it just last year, adapted by Jeffrey Hatcher and starring Mark-Linn Baker.
And in director Brandon J. Dirden’s misfired Roundabout Theatre Company revival, which opened Thursday night, the actors work very, very hard to make up for it.
Invalid—adapted by and starring Irwin, directed by Brandon J. Dirden—is an absolute delight.
Curiously, the role of crabby Argan is not entirely suited to Irwin's joyful nature and abilities.

As a New Yorker headline rightly reminded us just this week, Bill Irwin is “The OG Clown.” The legendary performer is also a perfect fit to portray self-pitying hypochondriac Monsieur Argan in Molière's farcical comedy The Imaginary Invalid, now receiving an enjoyable revival under the auspices of Roundabout Theatre Company.

If Irwin's adaptation of 'The Imaginary Invalid,' directed by Brandon J. Dirden, is too stylized for many of the laughs to have landed for me, Moliere's excoriating satire about doctors and the medical profession still resonates.
It just seems as though there is no clear vision behind this production.
So yes, this Invalid's heart is in the right place, but its funny bone is out of joint.
Dirden, makes passing references to AI and wellness culture, the 90-minute show emerges as dull as a medical waiting room.
This revival of 'The Imaginary Invalid' has a bad case of anemia despite Brandon J. Dirden directing the Moliere classic as if it were a screwball comedy.
In a spectacular Broadway debut, Rachel Bloom (Crazy Ex-Girlfriend) matches him as the sharp-witted maid Toinette, grounding this existential absurdity with her own bawdy glee.
You may find yourself smiling in acknowledgement of the cast's work more than laughing outright.
Staging Invalid as a herky-jerky puppet show does not disguise the fact that we are watching a play about the fear of death.

cn.t: Irwin's lush, visually stunning revival of Molière's medical satire earns mixed reviews, with critics praising the gorgeous design and star clown's performance while many find the comedy too stylized, with laughs landing unevenly.

vr.q: It's a very safe and by the book telling of a story that's humorous, but not inherently eventful enough to sustain 90 minutes.
